payload.title: Mohan Lal v. State of Rajasthan
payload.subtitle: High Court · Criminal

legal_issues: Whether the conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code can be sustained on the testimony of interested eyewitnesses, in the absence of independent corroboration?
Whether the delay of eleven hours in lodging the FIR, without a satisfactory explanation, is fatal to the prosecution's case?
Whether the recovery of the weapon under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act can be relied upon when the independent panch witness has turned hostile?
Whether the facts as proved make out an offence under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code rather than under Section 302?
key_facts: The prosecution case is that on the night of 9 July 2021 the deceased, Gopal Singh, was returning from his field to the village of Kanera when he was waylaid near the canal culvert at about ten in the night.

The families of the deceased and the appellant had been in a long-running dispute over the use of a shared irrigation channel, and a complaint about it had been made to the Sarpanch barely a week earlier.

It is alleged that the appellant and a co-accused, Hari Ram, who was declared a proclaimed offender and has not been tried, attacked the deceased with a kulhari (axe) and a lathi, and fled towards the fields. 3.

PW-1, Dhanna Singh, the brother of the deceased, deposed that he was walking about fifty paces behind the deceased and saw the appellant strike the deceased on the head with a kulhari while the co-accused hit him with a lathi.
Both witnesses admitted in cross-examination that they were related to the deceased and that they had a pending civil dispute with the appellant's family over the irrigation channel.
The First Information Report was lodged by PW-1 at Police Station Kanera at 9.15 a.m. on 10 July 2021, a delay of eleven hours after the occurrence.

On 12 July 2021 the appellant was arrested and, according to the prosecution, made a disclosure statement under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act leading to the recovery of a kulhari from a heap of dung cakes behind his house.

The Forensic Science Laboratory report recorded human blood of group B on the kulhari, the same group as the deceased, but the weapon was not sealed at the spot in the presence of any independent person and its chain of custody to the malkhana is not clearly established. 7.
profile.relief_sought: this Hon'ble Court set aside the judgment of conviction and sentence under Sections 302 read with 34 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code and acquit him of all charges, or in the alternative convict him under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code and reduce the sentence accordingly.

The appellant respectfully prays that this Hon'ble Court set aside the judgment of conviction and sentence under Sections 302 read with 34 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code and acquit him of all charges, or in the alternative convict him under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code and reduce the sentence accordingly.

The appellant respectfully submits that the conviction rests wholly on interested eyewitnesses without independent corroboration, that the recovery of the weapon is vitiated by the hostility of the independent panch witness and the doubtful chain of custody, that the eleven-hour delay in lodging the FIR remains unexplained in a matter involving admitted enmity, and that the learned trial court failed to consider the lesser offence.

The following questions arise for consideration before this Court:

Whether the conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code can be sustained on the testimony of interested eyewitnesses, in the absence of independent corroboration?
Whether the delay of eleven hours in lodging the FIR, without a satisfactory explanation, is fatal to the prosecution's case?
Whether the recovery of the weapon under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act can be relied upon when the independent panch witness has turned hostile?
Whether the facts as proved make out an offence under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code rather than under Section 302?

7. In his statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the appellant denied the prosecution case, stated that he was falsely implicated because of the irrigation dispute, and said that he was attending a wedding at Mandal on the night of 9 July 2021. One defence witness, DW-1, supported the wedding but could not name the guests who had seen the appellant there. The learned trial court rejected the plea of alibi as unproved and held that the testimony of PW-1 and PW-2, though related witnesses, was natural, consistent and corroborated by the medical evidence and the recovery. The court did not consider the plea that, on the prosecution's own case, the attack may have followed a sudden quarrel over the water channel.

8. The appellant respectfully submits that the conviction rests wholly on interested eyewitnesses without independent corroboration, that the recovery of the weapon is vitiated by the hostility of the independent panch witness and the doubtful chain of custody, that the eleven-hour delay in lodging the FIR remains unexplained in a matter involving admitted enmity,

The explanation offered was that PW-1 stayed with the body through the night because he feared that wild animals would disturb it, that the police station is eighteen kilometres from the village, and that the approach road was flooded after heavy rain. The learned trial court accepted this explanation in part. The appellant contends that the delay allowed time for deliberation and false implication, particularly given the admitted enmity.

The doctor was not asked whether the injuries could have been caused in a sudden fight rather than a premeditated attack.

6. On 12 July 2021 the appellant was arrested and, according to the prosecution, made a disclosure statement under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act leading to the recovery of a kulhari from a heap of dung cakes behind his house. PW-4, Kishan Lal, the independent witness to the recovery memo, turned hostile and denied having signed it at the spot; the recovery was proved only through the Investigating Officer, PW-5, Sub-Inspector Prakash Chand, and a police constable. The Forensic Science Laboratory report recorded human blood of group B on the kulhari, the same group as the deceased, but the weapon was not sealed at the spot in the presence of any independent person and its chain of custody to the malkhana is not clearly established.
